question.text: A scheduled commercial bank acquires shares of a listed company in the ordinary course of its lending business. Under what condition is this acquisition exempt from triggering an open offer?

answer.text: The bank must sell the shares within 6 months
The bank must not exercise voting rights beyond 1 year from the date of acquisition
The bank must not acquire more than 10% of the target company
The bank must obtain prior SEBI approval for each acquisition

explanation.text: The Logic: The SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations carve out specific exemptions from the open-offer obligation for acquisitions made by scheduled commercial banks in the ordinary course of business. Where such an exemption is conditioned on the bank not exercising voting rights on the acquired shares beyond one year from the date of acquisition, the bank may hold the shares as a lender / pledgee without triggering an open offer, provided it refrains from exercising voting rights past the prescribed period. The Trap: A mandatory 6-month sale window is not the regulatory condition — the regulation focuses on voting rights and not on disposal timelines. A 10% acquisition cap describes the trigger threshold for an open offer, not the exemption condition. Requiring prior SEBI approval for each acquisition is inconsistent with the "ordinary course of business" exemption framework. Note: The cited pages of the NISM-Series-IX Merchant Banking workbook (p.42, p.200-p.201) list ordinary-course exemptions for scheduled commercial banks acting as escrow agent and for invocation of pledge by scheduled commercial banks or public financial institutions, but do not explicitly state the one-year voting-rights condition. The framing above is general SEBI Takeover Regulations knowledge applied to bank acquisitions.
